source.title: Scaling and renormalization in high-dimensional regression
source.authors: Alexander Atanasov; Jacob A. Zavatone-Veth; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and simulates double-descent behavior in high-dimensional ridge and random-feature regression, using analytic random-matrix methods rather than the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own regression analyses, its stated multiple-descent result, and its own plotted regularization and feature-noise results. Results merely cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper derives and simulates where test error peaks and falls again in linear, kernel and random-feature ridge regression. It traces the peaks to specific variance terms and shows that a ridge can remove them. That is a different method aimed at V3, V4 and V6. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Roughly right but it misses the emphasis. The paper is mainly a unifying derivation. Using the S-transform and deterministic equivalence, sample-covariance fluctuations become a renormalized ridge. This yields training and test error, generalized-cross-validation estimators, and fine-grained bias-variance decompositions for linear, kernel and random-feature models. Its main novel results are scaling regimes, including a variance-dominated regime driven by initialization variance. Double descent is presented as one consequence of the renormalized ridge staying nonzero at zero explicit ridge.
record.recipe_differences: Analytic random-matrix and free-probability derivations, with regression simulations; the study does not reproduce the original deep-network training sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on covariance spectrum and structure, sample-to-dimension or width ratios, ridge strength, label noise, feature noise, and feature-weight structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Across linear and random-feature models, the peak condition is γ = (N/P)·df2(κ) → 1. Here df2 is a degrees-of-freedom measure. In the ridgeless limit this fixes the peak at P=N or P=Nℓ. The paper frames double descent as the effect of a renormalized ridge κ that stays nonzero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak occurs where a degrees-of-freedom ratio γ reaches 1. Implicit regularization from covariance fluctuations, a renormalized ridge, produces the second descent.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment
record.problems: The results are primarily asymptotic analyses under high-dimensional and random-matrix assumptions; simulations are limited to specified examples. The paper does not test epoch-wise descent or end-to-end deep-network model-size sweeps, and it does not establish optimal ridge tuning.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly relevant results were left out.

untested.parts: There are no end-to-end trained deep networks. The deep random-feature models train only the last layer.
No test error is reported over training epochs.
No test of whether one complexity measure places the peak across size, epochs and samples. The analytic peak condition γ = (N/P)·df2 → 1 appears but is not tested as such.
Whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak is not tested. Ridges are hand-chosen, or scaled as λ∼P^-l.
No re-plotting of the curve against an effective parameter count.
Only linear, kernel and random-feature regression are tested, not deep networks.

missing.what: Deep white random-feature ridgeless error has a divergence at P=D and at each P=Nℓ. These are multiple peaks, one per layer width.
missing.locator: Section IV.E.2 formula; Section IV.E.1, Fig. 6

missing.what: With the ridge scaled as λ∼P^-l, the P=N double-descent peak is eliminated, including with label noise σϵ=0.4.
With non-normalizable, slowly decaying spectra, γ→1 as P→N and error becomes nonmonotonic.
Nonlinear random features with isotropic data: ridgeless error formulas diverge at P=N, and simulations agree (40 seeds).

record.verdict_notes: The paper is largely a re-derivation of known results (Advani, Hastie, Canatar, Mel and Ganguli, Adlam and Pennington, Mei and Montanari), plus new bias-variance and scaling results. Its double-descent evidence is analytic, with matching simulations in specified figures. It does not test whether these mechanisms carry over to trained deep networks. The noiseless power-law analysis notes that explicit regularization hurts when there is no label noise. This is consistent with V6 but does not test optimal tuning when noise is present.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies linear and random-feature regression, not model-size sweeps in end-to-end deep networks.
No test-error trajectory over training epochs is reported; discussion of SGD dynamics refers to prior work.
The results concern specified ridge-regression and random-feature settings, not all data distributions or model classes.
The paper studies linear, kernel, and random-feature regression; it does not test all model classes or end-to-end deep networks.
Degrees of freedom and effective dimensionality are discussed, but the paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper does not establish that regularization is optimally tuned; it reports settings where a chosen ridge removes the peak.
No comparison shows that the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve when complexity is measured by an effective parameter count.

rows.subject: linear ridge regression
rows.operation_detail: Analyze generalization error as sample count P varies relative to N.

conditions.value: σϵ² as in the stated risk formula

rows.value: The text states that the error diverges at the interpolation threshold and gives different underparameterized and overparameterized expressions; the overparameterized expression is finite away from the threshold.
rows.locator: Section III.C, Eq. (25) and ridgeless-limit discussion; Section III.F; Fig. 1
rows.note: The paper also reports empirical agreement with theory in Fig. 1, with dots and error bars over 20 seeds.
rows.check: The value is accurate. The ridgeless divergence comes entirely from the σϵ² term. The noiseless overparameterized error is 1−P/N, which is finite. So this row also bears on V6's label-noise driver. Fig. 1 itself uses λ=1e-3 and σϵ=0.5, not the exact ridgeless limit.

rows.subject: linear regression with a gapped covariance spectrum
rows.size_stated: 10, 100, and 10000 modes across three spectral plateaus
rows.operation_detail: Analyze generalization error as sample count P varies across separated spectral plateaus.

conditions.value: increasing power in higher modes, given by 1, 10, 10²

rows.value: The text states that nonmonotonicity can occur as γ increases, producing multiple descents without label noise; Fig. 2 illustrates the result.
rows.note: The authors attribute the effect to variance over the sampled dataset and to unlearnable higher modes acting like effective noise.
rows.check: This is a sweep over sample count P, not over capacity, so the link to V4 should be dropped. It shows multiple peaks without label noise, driven by variance over the dataset (VarX) and by unlearnable modes acting as effective noise.

source_check.locator_found: Section III.G, Eqs. (27)–(28), and Fig. 2 caption.

rows.subject: deep structured linear random feature model
rows.stage_stated: random features; regression on final features
rows.operation_detail: Derive generalization error as feature-layer widths vary in the ridgeless overparameterized setting.
rows.measure: generalization error Eg and its variance components
rows.value: The authors state that model-wise double-descent peaks occur when any γ(ℓ) = 1 for ℓ ≥ 1, and identify the peak as due to feature-related variance terms.
rows.note: This is a theoretical result for random-feature regression, not a direct test on end-to-end deep networks.
rows.check: The cause is misattributed. The text says the model-wise peak at γ(ℓ)=1 is 'due entirely to the variances VarX,ϵ, VarX,F,ϵ'. These are label-noise interaction terms, not the feature-only variance. The sample-wise peak is due to VarX and VarX,ϵ. This is an analytic result only, with no simulation tied to it.

rows.operation_detail: Plot performance as P varies with ridge selected to eliminate the double-descent peak.

conditions.value: λ = 1e-05, chosen to eliminate the peak

rows.value: The figure caption states that the ridge has been chosen to eliminate the double-descent peak.
rows.note: The plotted curve is a ridge-regularized setting; the paper does not characterize the choice as an optimal tuning procedure.
rows.check: A ridge picked to remove the peak does remove it. The paper never shows the ridge is optimally tuned, so this bears only on 'regularization can remove the peak'.

rows.subject: random feature regression with additive feature noise
rows.stage_stated: random features; regression on noisy features
rows.operation_detail: Analyze performance as sample count P varies with feature noise and no explicit ridge.
rows.value: The text states that feature noise can mitigate label-noise effects, but a subsequent double-descent peak occurs without explicit ridge; the joint variance VarXFϵ is identified as its source.
rows.note: The figure caption notes less numerically stable empirical results near the peak.
rows.check: The row should also link to V3 (a peak in the P sweep at P=N, width N=5000) and to V4 (a nonlinear random-feature equivalent). Label noise σϵ=0.8 is present and the peak is attributed to VarX,F,ϵ. Feature noise acts as an effective ridge of order 1/P, but it does not remove the peak.

source_check.correct: Fig. 13(d) uses numerical ridge λ=10^-8, label noise σϵ=0.8, width N=5000, 25 datasets and 25 initializations. The caption describes the limiting interpretation as absence of explicit ridge. The sample-count sweep supports observed V3 and V6; this fixed-width experiment alone cannot determine V4's capacity-wise second descent.
